identity.title: Powered Industrial Truck Pre-Shift Inspection Log — Forklift FL-2 (Toyota 8FGU25, propane), September 2026, Portland Warehouse
identity.issuer: Cascade Specialty Chemicals, LLC (Portland Warehouse) — internal record completed by operators M.C. and J.R.

page_refs.issuer: page 1 header — 'CASCADE SPECIALTY CHEMICALS, LLC — PORTLAND WAREHOUSE'
page_refs.title: page 1 header — 'POWERED INDUSTRIAL TRUCK PRE-SHIFT INSPECTION LOG'

scan.summary: This is an internal inspection record — one month's worth of daily pre-use checks on a single propane forklift (unit FL-2) at the Portland warehouse, signed off by initials with an hour-meter reading and a 12-item checklist for each entry. A record like this is judged on whether it is complete and current, not against a written-program standard: it is the evidence you would hand an Oregon OSHA compliance officer to show the truck was examined before use, that defects were caught, and that the operators running it were certified. As it stands the sheet has days of use with no entry, one recorded defect with no resolution written next to it, no entries for the last week and a half, and an unsigned supervisor review line.
scan.freshness_note: Last entry is 2026-09-18, nine days before today (2026-09-27). The September sheet should be finished out and the October sheet opened; ask the warehouse supervisor for entries covering Sep 21–25 and Sep 28 onward, or an explanation that the truck did not run.

gaps.title: Days of use with no inspection entry (Sep 3 and Sep 4)
gaps.description: The log jumps from Sep 2 to Sep 7, but the hour meter climbed 15 hours over that break, so the truck was operated on days with no recorded examination. The document itself points this out.
gaps.fix: Do not back-fill. Find out who ran the truck on Sep 3–4 and why no sheet was completed, write a short dated note on the log explaining the omission, and put a control in place (sheet on the truck, supervisor checks it daily) so operation without a completed check is not possible.
gaps.citation: 29 CFR 1910.178(q)(7) — examine before placing in service, at least daily; adopted in Oregon by OAR 437-002-0220 with additional state rules at OAR 437-002-0227 (I am confident in the federal cite; the Oregon adoption cite I have checked but treat the OAR numbering as my best reading)
gaps.locator: page 1 table (gap between 'Sep 2' and 'Sep 7' rows); page 2 closing note
gaps.quote: The hour meter rises between Sep 2 (4,819) and Sep 7 (4,834), which shows the truck ran on the missing days.

gaps.title: Recorded defect with no repair or return-to-service record
gaps.description: On Sep 9 the horn was marked X with the note 'Horn not working'. There is nothing on the sheet showing the truck was taken out of service, who repaired the horn, or when it was returned to service — the Sep 10 row simply shows the horn ticked again.
gaps.fix: Attach the work order or mechanic's note for the horn repair to this month's sheet. Add a 'defect reported to / corrective action / date returned to service' block to the form so every X has a closing entry beside it.
gaps.citation: 29 CFR 1910.178(q)(7) (defects immediately reported and corrected) and 29 CFR 1910.178(p)(1) (truck taken out of service until restored to safe operating condition)

gaps.title: No entries for the last seven working days
gaps.description: The sheet stops at Sep 18. Sep 21 through Sep 25 were working weekdays and today is Sep 27, so either the truck sat idle for over a week or inspections were done and not written down.
gaps.fix: Complete the September sheet through month end or record that the truck was out of use, and confirm the October sheet is on the truck.

gaps.title: Supervisor review line left blank
gaps.description: The form provides for a supervisor sign-off and date; both are empty, so nothing shows the sheet was reviewed by anyone above the operators — which is how the two missing days and the unresolved horn defect went unchallenged.
gaps.fix: Have the warehouse supervisor review and sign the September sheet, noting the Sep 3–4 omission and the horn repair, and set a weekly review habit rather than month-end.

gaps.title: Only day-shift checks recorded at a site your records describe as multi-shift
gaps.description: Every row on this sheet is marked 'Day'. Your existing company record carries a fact that the site operates multiple shifts. If FL-2 is also driven on a second shift, that shift's use is not covered by any entry here.
gaps.fix: Confirm whether FL-2 is used outside day shift. If it is, add a row per shift (or an after-shift examination if the truck runs round-the-clock) and name the operator for each.
gaps.citation: 29 CFR 1910.178(q)(7) — trucks used on a round-the-clock basis examined after each shift

Forklift operator evaluation due — J. Rivera

facts.affects: Confirms 29 CFR 1910.178 (and Oregon's additional PIT rules) apply at the Portland site, bringing daily examination, operator training and certification duties.
Brings LP-gas cylinder storage, exchange and fire-code duties into play alongside forklift rules, and matters to fire-safety planning at a chemical warehouse.

expected_missing.why: A propane forklift means cylinder storage on a site that also stores solvents and corrosives.
expected_missing.basis: similar companies, not a checked requirement

expected_missing.basis: similar companies, not a checked requirement

scan.confidence_notes: High confidence on what the document is, whose it is, which site, and every quoted line — the sheet is legible and self-describing. High confidence that the missing Sep 3–4 entries, the unresolved Sep 9 horn defect and the blank supervisor line are real completeness problems; the document itself flags the first. The weekday reasoning for Sep 21–25 is inferred from the calendar, not read. High confidence on 29 CFR 1910.178(q)(7) and (p)(1) as the governing text and on the three-year operator evaluation cycle under 1910.178(l); moderate confidence on the exact Oregon adoption citations (OAR 437-002-0220 adoption by reference, OAR 437-002-0227 additional Oregon PIT rules) — the substance is federal either way, enforced in Oregon by Oregon OSHA. Worth knowing: OSHA has interpreted the standard as requiring the examination, not necessarily a written checklist — but once you keep a log, the gaps in it become the story an inspector reads, so the findings above still matter. I have not judged whether a second shift actually uses this truck; that comes from an existing company fact, not from this sheet.
